newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top Mideast, Russian figures going to Swiss meet.
newsitem.headline: Top Mideast, Russian figures going to Swiss meet.

text.p: Key leaders from the Middle East and the two top figures around ailing Russian President Boris Yeltsin will attend the annual World Economic Forum in Davos starting next week, the organisers announced on Tuesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak will all be there at the same time, although it was not yet certain that they would meet, Forum officials said.

From Moscow, Forum Executive Director Claude Smadja told a news conference, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and president chief of staff Anatoly Chubais would attend the 26-year-old gathering of world business and political leaders.
But Forum sources said that -- apparently in view of Yeltsin's long-running health problems and his current convalescence -- they would not be there at the same time.

Other prominent figures who have agreed to address this year's meeting -- from January 30 to February 4 -- are new United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan and Newt Gingrich, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives.

Gingrich, facing a $300,000 fine for admitted ethics violations, will speak at the Forum on Sunday February 2 in his first major speech abroad since he took up the key post following the Republican electoral victories of 1994.

A major theme at the meeting -- also attended by leading central and private bankers as well as top executives of major global companies -- will be European Monetary Union, Forum president and founder Klaus Schwab said.

Taking part in sessions on the single currency planned for 1999 and its implications for business and the world economy will be European Commission President Jacques Santer and finance ministers from several European Union member states.

These include German Finance Minister Theodor Waigel, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, France's Economy and Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Spain's Finance Minister Rodrigo Rato.

Other key financial figures present will be U.S. Under- Secretary of the Treasury Lawrence Summers, Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet, Howard Davies, deputy governor of the Bank of England, and Akira Nagashima, deputy governor of the Bank of Japan.

Three years ago, the Forum privided the backdrop for key talks between then Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Arafat which helped clear the way for the Middle East peace agreements known as the "Oslo accords."
But Schwab, a German academic who has wide contacts throughout the political and business world, said he was not attempting to arrange any formal talks involving Netanyahu and Arafat or Mubarak.

"At the Forum, we leave it to the people involved to arrange such meetings if they wish," he told reporters. Smadja said it was hoped all three would appear at a session on the Middle East and answer questions from the same platform.
Other issues on the wide-ranging Forum agenda this year include emerging markets and the extent to which they have to change policies to attract foreign investment.

Taking part in debates on this theme will be Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, South Africa's Deputy President Theo Mbeki and senior government and financial figures from former European communist countries and Latin America.

Another topic will be workers' rights in the global economy. Addressing a special session on this will be Bill Jordan, General Secretary of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) -- currently in South Korea to observe government handling of strikes there.
